section.title: Wisdom and Folly
section.sectionRationale: The tenth discourse closes the extended teaching of chapters 1 to 9 with two competing invitations to a feast. Wisdom builds a house and calls the simple to her table, verses 1 to 6, framing reflections on mockers and the wise around the book's motto restated, verses 7 to 12, before Folly builds a rival, empty invitation of her own, verses 13 to 18.
section.thesis: Two women call from their houses to the same simple passers by, Wisdom, offering a feast that leads to life and understanding, and Folly, offering stolen pleasure that leads to death, and every person must choose which table to sit at.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Wisdom's house, feast, and invitation, verses 1 to 6; reflections on mockers, the wise, and the restated motto of the book, verses 7 to 12; and Folly's rival house and empty invitation, verses 13 to 18.

verses.text: {{chokmah|Wisdom}} has built her house; she has carved out her seven pillars.
She has prepared her meat and mixed her wine; she has also set her table.
She has sent out her maidservants; she calls out from the heights of the city.
"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" she says to him who lacks judgment.
"Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed.
Leave your folly behind, and you will live; walk in the way of understanding."

units.label: Mockers, the wise, and the book's motto restated
units.note: the fear of the LORD, again

verses.text: He who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself; he who rebukes a wicked man taints himself.
Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.
Instruct a wise man, and he will be wiser still; teach a righteous man, and he will increase his learning.
The {{yirah|fear of the LORD}} is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
For through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.
If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage; but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.
The woman named {{kesiluth|Folly}} is loud; she is naive and knows nothing.
She sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the heights of the city,
calling out to those who pass by, who make their paths straight.
"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" she says to him who lacks judgment.
"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!"
But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, pictured here as a gracious hostess who builds a substantial house, prepares a full feast, and sends servants to call the simple to her table freely. Her invitation costs the guest nothing but is bought at her own expense, offering life and understanding to anyone who will come.

yirah.gloss: The fear of the LORD, restated here in verse 10 in almost the same words as the book's opening motto in 1:7, forming bookends around the whole first section of Proverbs and confirming that everything taught in chapters 1 to 9 flows from this one root.

kesiluth.gloss: Folly, personified as a rival woman who mimics Wisdom's invitation with an almost identical call, whoever is simple, let him turn in here, but offers only stolen pleasure that conceals a house full of the dead.

basic.context: This chapter closes the long teaching section of Proverbs 1 to 9 with a vivid contrast. Wisdom builds a grand house, prepares a real feast, and sends servants to invite the simple in, promising life and understanding to anyone who comes. Folly mimics this same invitation almost word for word, but her house hides death, and her guests do not realize until too late that they have joined the dead in Sheol. In between stands a reflection on how mockers and the wise respond so differently to correction, anchored by the restatement of the book's opening motto, the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
basic.hermeneutics: The deliberate echo between Wisdom's invitation, verse 4, and Folly's invitation, verse 16, whoever is simple, let him turn in here, is the key to reading this chapter. Both call to the same undecided people; the difference is entirely in what lies behind the door. This teaches that temptation rarely looks obviously evil, it imitates the language of what is good, and only the fear of the LORD, restated at the chapter's center, verse 10, equips a person to tell the two houses apart.
basic.originalLanguages: Chokmah, wisdom, here builds and hosts like a substantial noblewoman, sparing no expense on her seven pillared house and prepared feast. The chapter's center restates yirah, the fear of the LORD, in language nearly identical to 1:7, binding the whole first section of the book together around this one motto. And kesiluth, folly, is personified as wisdom's dark twin, using the very same words of invitation to lure the same simple passers by toward death instead of life.
basic.typology: Wisdom's free invitation, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed, verse 5, anticipates the gospel's own invitation to a costly feast freely offered, most directly Isaiah's call, come, buy wine and milk without money, Isaiah 55:1, and Christ's own words, I am the bread of life, John 6:35.
basic.christ: Wisdom's invitation in this chapter, come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed, and leave your folly behind and live, is a striking foreshadowing of Christ's own invitation. He identifies Himself as the bread of life, John 6:35, and offers His body and blood at a table prepared at great cost to Him, so that all who come, however simple or lacking in judgment, might truly live. Where Wisdom's house in Proverbs is one image among several, in Christ the invitation, the host, and the feast itself are united in a single person.
basic.god: God, through Wisdom's picture, is generous and hospitable, sparing no expense to prepare a feast and going out of His way to call in the simple and undiscerning, not only the already wise. He is also just, allowing genuine consequences to fall on those who choose the rival house, so that scoffers alone bear what their own choice brings, verse 12.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 55:1 to 2 issues a strikingly similar invitation, come, buy wine and milk without money, echoing Wisdom's free feast. John 6:35 has Christ call Himself the bread of life. Matthew 22:1 to 14 pictures the kingdom as a wedding feast to which all are invited. Revelation 19:9 calls the redeemed blessed who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.
basic.oneStory: Two houses, two feasts, two invitations using almost the same words, this chapter's picture captures the whole of life's central choice, and the whole Bible's central invitation. That invitation reaches its fullest form in Christ, who offers Himself as the bread of life at a table prepared at His own cost, calling even the simple and undiscerning to leave folly behind and live.

context.literary:
Count the verses and the design shows. Proverbs 9 falls into three panels of exactly six verses each: Wisdom's house and call, verses 1 to 6, the reflection on mockers and the wise, verses 7 to 12, and Folly's house and call, verses 13 to 18. The outer panels are mirrors. Each woman has a house, each sits or stands in the high places of the city, verses 3 and 14, and each speaks the same invitation, 'Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!', verses 4 and 16, to 'him who lacks judgment.' The two panels are the same sentence set to opposite menus.

The differences are what the reader is meant to catch. Wisdom's verbs are all finished work: she 'has built,' 'has carved out,' 'has prepared,' 'has mixed,' 'has set,' 'has sent.' Everything is ready before anyone arrives. Folly has no verbs of preparation at all. She 'sits,' she 'calls,' and her menu is a line of stolen water and bread eaten in secret, verse 17, against Wisdom's meat, wine and a laid table. Wisdom sends servants; Folly does her own calling. Wisdom's guests are told to 'leave your folly behind' and live, verse 6, while Folly's ends in the depths of Sheol, verse 18.

The middle panel is the hinge. It has the shape of a sequence of proverbs set between two speeches, and it carries the reason the choice matters: the mocker will turn on his corrector, the wise man will grow, and the whole matter rests on 'the fear of the LORD,' verse 10. That verse closes the circle begun in 1:7, so that chapters 1 to 9 are bracketed by one motto. Chapter 9 is also the last word of the book's prologue. The next verse begins the short sayings of Solomon, which assume that the reader has already chosen a table.
context.historical:
A feast in the ancient world was prepared and announced in a set order. The host slaughtered the animals, mixed the wine, set the table, and then sent servants out to call the guests, just as Wisdom does in verses 2 and 3. The sequence appears in Jesus' parable of the great banquet, where the servant says 'Come, for everything is now ready,' Luke 14:17. Wisdom's meal is a meal for those who have not earned a place at it, which is why the invitation goes out to the simple and to those who lack judgment.

The 'seven pillars' of verse 1 suggest a house on a grand scale. Solomon's House of the Forest of Lebanon had four rows of cedar pillars supporting the beams, 1 Kings 7:2 and 3, and in Israel's building the pillar was a sign of wealth and permanence. Seven, throughout Scripture, is the number of completeness. The verb 'carved out' is the one used of hewing rock from a quarry, Isaiah 51:1, so the pillars are not painted on but cut from stone.

The 'mixed' wine, verse 2, was wine prepared with spices, as in Psalm 75:8, a host's lavish extravagance and not the everyday cup. The meal tells the guest that the host has spared nothing. Folly's table has no such cost. Her menu of 'stolen water' and 'bread eaten in secret' belongs to a world of covert appetite. The first hearers would have recognised water as a common picture for marital intimacy, Proverbs 5:15 to 17, so her offer is the thrill of what is forbidden, and the proverb elsewhere warns that food gained by fraud tastes sweet and then fills the mouth with gravel, Proverbs 20:17.

The mocker was a recognisable figure in Israel's life. Proverbs 21:24 calls 'Mocker' the name of the proud and arrogant man, and 29:8 says mockers inflame a city. In a small town a scoffer could poison a gathering, so the sage's counsel not to waste correction on such a man is a practical rule for a society that depended on its neighbours' goodwill. The last line of the chapter reaches for the other side of the town, the dead, who in Israel's imagination waited in Sheol.
context.canonical:
Verse 10 is the best known sentence of the chapter and one of the best known in the Old Testament. It has a long afterlife. Psalm 111:10 repeats it, 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom,' Job 28:28 makes it the answer to the search for wisdom, and Ecclesiastes 12:13 closes that book with 'Fear God and keep His commandments.' The sage who wrote the prologue and the preacher who wrote the epilogue of Ecclesiastes agree on the starting point.

The picture of two tables carries through the prophets. Isaiah 55:1 to 3 invites the thirsty to come to the waters and eat what is good, 'without money and without cost,' and Isaiah 25:6 promises a banquet on the mountain for all peoples. Isaiah 65:13 sets servants who eat against rebels who go hungry. The same contrast lies behind the Psalms' image of the table prepared by the LORD, Psalm 23:5.

The New Testament takes up the idea of an invitation that some refuse. Jesus tells of the great banquet to which the invited make excuses and the poor are brought in, Luke 14:15 to 24, and of the king's wedding banquet, Matthew 22:1 to 4. He speaks of Himself as the bread from heaven, John 6:35 and 51, and as the one who stands at the door and knocks, Revelation 3:20. Paul draws the sharpest line when he says 'you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too,' 1 Corinthians 10:21, which is the choice of Proverbs 9 stated in the language of the church. Revelation finishes the contrast with two suppers, the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, and the grim supper to which the birds are called, Revelation 19:17 and 18. Jesus also takes up Wisdom's voice: 'wisdom is vindicated by all her children,' Luke 7:35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage wanted the reader to leave chapters 1 to 9 with a choice that cannot be dodged. After eight chapters of instruction the question is no longer what wisdom is but whose house a person walks into. The repeated invitation puts the reader in the place of the young man on the street, and the identical wording means that he cannot tell the houses apart by what is said at the door. He must tell them by what he knows of the one who speaks, and by what he does with his fear of the LORD.

The central verses, 7 to 12, give two things a person needs to choose well. One is a teachable heart. The mocker cannot learn because correction offends him, while the wise man treats it as a gift. The other is the fear of the LORD, which the sage insists is the starting point and not an extra. Wisdom without that fear is just cleverness, and cleverness is exactly what a smooth voice at the door of Folly would flatter.

The final verse is meant to land hard. 'They do not know,' verse 18, is a verdict on the guests, not on Folly, who knows nothing herself, verse 13. The sage is not trying to scare the reader into a technique. He is trying to expose the lack of knowledge that lets a person eat stolen bread with a smile, and to send him back to the other table with fear and joy.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The two scenes describe invitations that are made, and the prescription sits in the middle. Verse 6 is the one direct command to the simple: leave your folly behind, and walk in the way of understanding. Verses 7 to 9 give advice for dealing with other people, and verses 10 to 12 state the principle. Folly's call is recorded so that it can be recognised, not so that anyone follows it.

Two cautions help in applying the chapter. First, the counsel not to rebuke a mocker, verses 7 and 8, is a general observation about how such a person reacts, and the chapter does not forbid all correction. Elsewhere the same book commends the rebuke of a friend, Proverbs 27:5 and 6, and the New Testament asks for gentle correction of those who oppose the truth, 2 Timothy 2:24 to 26. The proverb is about where to spend breath, not about abandoning anyone. Second, the promise of long life in verse 11 describes how wisdom tends to bear out, as in Proverbs 3:1 and 2, and not a guarantee for every individual. The principle of verse 12, that each person carries their own choice, stands without exception.

debates.question: Are verses 7 to 12 part of the original design, or a displaced insertion?

views.label: An interruption
views.case: Some scholars notice that the verses on mockers and the wise sound like the short sayings of chapters 10 and following and seem to break the flow between the two women. They suggest the verses were moved here or added by an editor.

views.label: A deliberate hinge
views.case: The three panels have six verses each, which suggests a planned design. The sayings in the middle explain what a person needs to be able to choose between the two tables, a teachable heart and the fear of the LORD, and they restate the motto of 1:7 so that the prologue closes where it began. Without them the chapter would show two invitations and no way to tell them apart.

debates.bearing: The structure of six, six and six, and the way verse 10 answers 1:7, favour the hinge reading. Even if an editor shaped the chapter, the final form teaches the same lesson, that discernment between two tables is a matter of both heart and fear.

debates.question: Does verse 8 forbid correcting a scoffer?

views.label: Never rebuke a scoffer
views.case: The verse says plainly, 'Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you.' Jesus gives a similar rule in Matthew 7:6 about not giving what is holy to dogs or throwing pearls before swine, and Proverbs 22:10 tells the community to drive out the mocker so that conflict will leave.

views.label: Sometimes correct him for the sake of others
views.case: Proverbs 19:25 says that when a mocker is struck, 'the simple will beware.' Correction may do nothing for the scorner but warns the onlookers. The New Testament also asks for patient, gentle reproof of opponents in case God grants repentance, 2 Timothy 2:24 to 26, and gives a process for a brother who refuses to listen, Matthew 18:15 to 17.

views.label: Discern the person
views.case: The proverb is a rule of thumb about types. The same book pairs 26:4 and 5, 'Do not answer a fool according to his folly' and 'Answer a fool according to his folly,' to teach that no single rule fits every case and that wisdom is knowing which response the moment needs.

debates.bearing: The verse tells the reader what to expect from a mocker, and it tells the wise man where his effort is best spent. It does not remove the duty to speak when the truth must be told for the sake of others or for the sake of the person himself, and it should be held with the other proverbs.

debates.question: What do the seven pillars mean?

views.label: Completeness
views.case: Seven is the biblical number of fullness, so the house is a perfect, finished work, and Wisdom has left nothing undone.

views.label: The days of creation
views.case: Because Proverbs 3:19 and 8:22 to 31 tie Wisdom to the making of the world, some read the seven pillars as the seven days of creation, so that her house is the ordered cosmos.

views.label: A grand building
views.case: Others take the pillars as part of the picture of a wealthy house with a large hall, without any symbolism, as in Solomon's House of the Forest of Lebanon, 1 Kings 7:2 and 3.

debates.bearing: The poem does not tell us, and the lesson does not depend on the answer. Whichever view is taken, the house is complete, costly and ready for guests, and that is the point of the contrast with Folly, who has built nothing.

study.originalLanguages:
Wisdom in verse 1 is chokhmot, a plural form of the word, which also appears in Proverbs 1:20. The plural is usually understood as an intensive, not as many wisdoms, and gives her a note of fullness and majesty. The verb 'carved out' is chatsvah, to hew, the word used for stone cut from a quarry in Isaiah 51:1, which makes the pillars solid, not decorative. The preparations of verse 2 are written with the root tabach, 'to slaughter,' a word used for slaughter for a meal as in Genesis 43:16, 'Slaughter an animal and prepare it.' Wisdom does not offer a snack. She has killed and cooked.

The expression 'lacks judgment' in verses 4 and 16 is chasar lev, literally 'lacking heart.' The same phrase describes the young man in Proverbs 7:7 and the adulterer in 6:32. In Hebrew thought the heart was the seat of decision, so this is the person who lacks the capacity to weigh. Wisdom and Folly are speaking to the same person with exactly the same words, and the only difference is what lies behind the door.

Verse 7 uses two verbs of correction, one from the root meaning to discipline and instruct for the 'corrects,' and one from the usual root for rebuke for the 'rebukes,' and verse 8 repeats the second. The mocker, lets, is the proud person of Proverbs 21:24, and the penalty for rebuking him is that the corrector 'taints himself.' The Hebrew has a noun, mum, 'blemish,' the word for the defect that disqualified an animal from sacrifice. Correcting a scoffer, says the sage, leaves a stain on the corrector.

The restatement of the motto in verse 10 differs slightly from 1:7. There it is 'the beginning of knowledge,' using a noun that means the first and chief part, and here it is 'the beginning of wisdom,' with a different noun meaning the starting point, as in Psalm 111:10. The second line speaks of 'knowledge of the Holy One,' where the Hebrew noun for Holy One is plural, a plural of majesty, as in Proverbs 30:3. Knowing God as holy is the understanding the chapter points to.

Verse 12 contains a verb of carrying: the scoffer 'alone' will 'bear' it, from the verb that elsewhere means to bear sin or to bear a burden. The BSB's 'consequences' hides a Hebrew image of someone lifting a load that is entirely his own. The BSB footnote on verse 11 records that the Greek, Syriac and Aramaic read 'through wisdom' where the Hebrew has 'through me,' so the Hebrew has Wisdom herself speaking in the middle panel, in the manner of 3:2 and 4:10.

The woman of verse 13 is literally 'the woman of folly,' eshet kesilut, a construct phrase like 'the woman of valor,' eshet chayil, in Proverbs 31:10, so the BSB's 'named Folly' is an interpretation. She is 'loud,' hamiyyah, the very word used of the adulteress in Proverbs 7:11, which ties her to the woman of chapter 7. Verse 15 adds that she calls to those 'who make their paths straight,' so she targets people who are already on the right road. The BSB footnote on verse 18 notes that the Hebrew has 'the Rephaim,' the shades of the dead, as in Isaiah 14:9 and Proverbs 21:16, and not simply 'the dead.'

typology.fulfillment: Wisdom builds a house, prepares a feast and invites the simple to eat her bread and drink her wine. Jesus says 'I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever,' John 6:51, and at the last supper takes bread and wine and says 'This is My body' and 'This is My blood of the covenant,' Mark 14:22 to 24. Paul calls the cup and the bread participation in Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:16. The escalation is that the host is also the meal. The type falls short because Wisdom provides food, while Christ gives Himself, at the cost of His life.

typology.type: The servants sent to call the guests, 9:3
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom sends out her maidservants to call from the high places. In Jesus' parable the king sends servants to call the invited to the wedding banquet, Matthew 22:3 and 4, and the master of the great banquet sends his servant to say 'Come, for everything is now ready,' Luke 14:17. The sending of messengers becomes the church's task, as Paul says, 'we are ambassadors for Christ,' 2 Corinthians 5:20. The pattern is real and the escalation is that the invitation now goes to all nations. The type falls short because the servants of Proverbs call the simple of Israel, while Christ's servants call everyone.

The two houses present one choice in two forms. Paul speaks in the same terms when he says 'You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too,' 1 Corinthians 10:21, and Revelation shows the marriage supper of the Lamb beside the gruesome supper that awaits the beast's armies, Revelation 19:9 and 17 and 18. The correspondence sharpens: a decision about a table is a decision about a master. It is a pattern more than a prediction, and it falls short in that the end of the age places both tables in their final settings.

Folly's 'stolen water' and 'bread eaten in secret' picture pleasure taken in the dark. Hebrews says that Moses chose to suffer with God's people 'rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin,' Hebrews 11:25, and Paul asks what fruit the old life bore, 'the outcome of those things is death,' Romans 6:21. In Christ the contrast is complete: He offers freely what Folly steals, and He pays for what we took. The type is a warning more than a promise, and it falls short in that the New Testament offers a way back for the guests of Folly, while the proverb ends in Sheol.

study.christ:
The chapter meets Christ by an invitation that cannot be earned. Wisdom does not ask the guests to bring anything. She has built, killed, mixed and set the table before anyone arrives, and the only ones she calls are those who know they are simple. Jesus describes His ministry in the same pattern. He says He came not for the righteous but for sinners, and He tells of a banquet whose guests are the poor, the crippled and the blind, Luke 14:21. The Gospels' pictures of Jesus eating with sinners are Wisdom's table in practice, and He answers the criticism with the line 'wisdom is vindicated by her actions,' Matthew 11:19.

It meets Christ in the person of the host who is also the food. Wisdom's bread and mixed wine foreshadow, in the only way an Old Testament poem can, the table in which the host gives Himself. Jesus says 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, and 'My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink,' John 6:55, and at the Passover meal He gives the disciples bread and a cup as His body and the blood of the covenant, Mark 14:22 to 24. Believers differ over how the Lord's Supper should be understood, but all agree that it is a meal in which Christ is the one who feeds, not only the one who invites.

It meets Christ in the call to leave folly and live. Wisdom's invitation in verse 6 carries two verbs, leave and walk. Jesus' first words in Mark are a call to repent and believe, and His disciples are those who leave and follow. Hebrews says Moses chose the people of God over 'the fleeting enjoyment of sin,' Hebrews 11:25, and Christ is the one who makes that exchange possible.

And it meets Christ at the foot of the other table. Folly's guests do not know 'that the dead are there.' Yet Jesus, who comes to those who are dead, offers the end of that road with a different outcome. He says 'Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day,' John 6:54. The grave that Folly hides is the one He opens.

One caution keeps this honest. The chapter does not call Wisdom the Son, and it never speaks of her death or of a body and blood. The links come from Jesus' own use of banquet and wisdom language, from Paul's reading of the cross as the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, and from the shape of the choice the gospel puts to every hearer.
study.god:
The God behind this chapter is a host who prepares in full before He invites. Wisdom's house is built, her meat is cooked and her table is set, so the God she speaks for does not call people to a half-ready work. Everything needed for life is supplied before a guest crosses the threshold. That is the shape of grace: the provision comes first, the invitation second, and the guest brings nothing but need.

He is generous to the lowest. The invitation goes to the simple and those who lack judgment, which means that wisdom is open to anyone who will turn in. In a world that gave learning to the privileged, this God sends servants through the streets. He does not wait for the capable. The same generosity runs through Isaiah 55:1, where the thirsty with no money are told to come and buy.

He is holy, and the fear He asks for is the start of wisdom. Verse 10 names Him 'the Holy One,' and the plural in the Hebrew conveys the fullness of that holiness. The fear of the LORD is not terror of a tyrant but the recognition that He is who He is and that all understanding begins by taking Him at His word. This is why the whole prologue of the book ends here. A person cannot tell the two houses apart without it.

He is just in a way that respects human choice. Verse 12 says the scoffer alone bears the result, and the final scene shows Folly's guests unaware of where they are. God does not drag anyone into either house. Yet His justice is not cold: the warning is spoken into the street so that no one can say he was not told, and the same Wisdom calls in Proverbs 1:20 to 23, offering to pour out her spirit on those who turn. The judgment that follows a refusal, Proverbs 1:24 to 33, is described as the fruit of the person's own way.

For worship, the chapter gives two postures. One is gratitude that the table is already set, for we did not build it. The other is the quiet fear that listens to correction and does not take offense, since the wise man loves the one who rebukes him. We come to the feast as guests, and we leave the stolen bread behind.

crossReferences.note: The motto at the head of the book reads 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' Proverbs 9:10 restates it with 'wisdom' in place of 'knowledge,' bracketing chapters 1 to 9 into one unit. The prologue ends where it began, which tells the reader that every lecture between them was an unpacking of this one sentence.

Wisdom calls in the street and the square, at the city gates, and pleads with the simple to turn. Chapter 9 shows the same call from her house, now with a prepared feast. The earlier passage supplies the warning, and the later one the welcome, so the two are the left and right hands of one invitation.

The father says to drink water from your own cistern and keep the springs for yourself, rather than being captivated by an adulteress. Folly's 'stolen water' in 9:17 is the same water taken from another's well. Her sweetness is the sweetness of the forbidden, which the earlier passage has already described as theft from one's own marriage.

The woman who meets the young man is loud and brazen, and she seizes him. Folly in 9:13 is 'loud,' with the same Hebrew word, and her invitation uses the same bait. The two chapters are meant to be read together, so that the adulteress of chapter 7 is revealed as Folly in the flesh.

Wisdom's last words in chapter 8 say that those who find her find life and that those who hate her love death. Chapter 9 puts a table under that statement. The two chapters are one scene: Wisdom speaks, and then she sets her table, and Folly's counter-invitation shows what 'loving death' looks like.

The psalm repeats the motto of Proverbs 9:10 and adds that those who follow His precepts gain rich understanding. It shows that the fear of the LORD was a common creed in Israel's worship, not only a teacher's maxim, and that it leads to action as well as to attitude.

The LORD invites the thirsty and the penniless to come, eat and drink without cost, and to listen so that their souls may live. The verbs match Wisdom's 'come, eat my bread and drink the wine.' Isaiah adds that the feast rests on an everlasting covenant, which shows what stands behind Wisdom's generosity.

Jesus tells of a man who prepared a great banquet and sent his servant to say that everything was ready. Those invited made excuses, and the poor and the crippled were brought in. The parable follows the plot of Proverbs 9: a prepared table, a call, a refusal by some, and welcome for those who know their need.

Paul teaches that the cup and bread of the Lord are a participation in Christ, and that one cannot also take the cup and table of demons. This is the choice of Proverbs 9 in the life of a church. Two tables mean two fellowships, and no one sits at both.

Jesus calls Himself the living bread and says that whoever eats of it will live forever. Wisdom's 'eat my bread' in verse 5 is here answered by a host who offers Himself. The promise of life that Wisdom attaches to her bread in verse 6 is given by Christ in full measure.

The bride has made herself ready, and the blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. This is the last and fullest form of Wisdom's feast. It also stands opposite Folly's table, because Revelation 17 shows the great prostitute and Revelation 19 shows her end.

Christ stands at the door and knocks, offering to come in and dine with anyone who opens. Wisdom calls from the heights and Christ calls from the door, but the offer is the same, fellowship at a table. It also shows that the invitation continues to be spoken to churches that have grown comfortable.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden in which God gives food freely from every tree and sets one tree apart. The first temptation arrives as a promise that the forbidden fruit is good, Genesis 3:6, and the first humans take what they were not given. Proverbs 9 distils that moment into two tables. Wisdom lays out a feast and Folly offers stolen water. Every later temptation in the Bible is a version of the second table dressed up as the first, which is why the sage insists the guests cannot tell by the invitation alone.

The story that follows is of a God who keeps setting a table. He feeds Israel in the wilderness, sets a banquet in the presence of enemies, Psalm 23:5, and promises through Isaiah a feast on the mountain for all peoples, where death itself will be swallowed up, Isaiah 25:6 to 8. Israel's history is partly a record of choosing the wrong table, and the prophets say so, Isaiah 65:13. Yet the invitation is repeated: 'Come, buy wine and milk without money,' Isaiah 55:1.

In Christ the invitation is fulfilled. He eats with sinners, gives bread to the crowds, and at the last supper gives Himself under the signs of bread and wine, Mark 14:22 to 25. He says to the weary 'Come to Me,' Matthew 11:28, and He stands at the door of a lukewarm church and knocks, Revelation 3:20. The refusal that Folly's guests make unknowingly is met by a host who goes out looking, and who pays for the feast with His own life.

The story ends at a supper. 'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. Folly's house, with its stolen bread and its dead guests, is gone along with the great prostitute of Revelation 17, and the Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The tree of life is open, the river runs, and the table that Wisdom set in the heights of the city is set at last in the city that God builds, Revelation 21:2 and 22:2.

quiz.q: What has Wisdom done to prepare for her guests, according to verses 1 to 5?

options.text: Built a substantial house, prepared a full feast, and sent servants to call in the simple.
options.note: All three details, house, feast, and servants sent to invite, appear directly in the text.

options.text: Hidden herself away from public view.
options.note: The passage stresses her public, active invitation, the opposite of hiding.

options.text: Charged a high entrance fee for her feast.
options.note: The passage presents her feast as an open invitation, not a paid entry.

options.text: Invited only the already wise and accomplished.
options.note: The text specifically targets 'whoever is simple' and 'him who lacks judgment,' not only the already wise.

quiz.q: What does verse 10 restate, and where else does this appear?

options.text: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, echoing the book's opening motto in 1:7.
options.note: This near identical restatement forms a literary bracket around chapters 1 to 9.

options.text: A completely new teaching never mentioned before in the book.
options.note: It is a deliberate restatement of the book's opening motto, not a new idea.

options.text: A warning specific to kings alone.
options.note: The statement is general, addressed to any reader, not restricted to kings.

options.text: A minor detail with little significance to the book's structure.
options.note: This understates its role; the near verbatim repetition deliberately brackets the entire first section of Proverbs.

quiz.q: How does Folly's invitation in verse 16 compare to Wisdom's in verse 4?

options.text: It uses almost identical words, showing that temptation often mimics what is good rather than looking obviously evil.
options.note: Both verses use the same phrase, 'Whoever is simple, let him turn in here,' making this parallel deliberate.

options.text: It is obviously different and easy to distinguish at a glance.
options.note: The passage's power lies precisely in how similar the two invitations sound.

options.text: It targets a completely different audience.
options.note: Both invitations target the same simple, undiscerning passers by.

options.text: It offers a more expensive and lavish feast than Wisdom's.
options.note: Folly's offering is described as stolen and secret, not lavish or costly like Wisdom's prepared feast.

quiz.q: What is the hidden reality behind Folly's house, according to verse 18?

options.text: Her guests do not realize that the dead are there, in the depths of Sheol.
options.note: This is the chapter's final, sobering revelation.

options.text: Her house is simply empty and harmless.
options.note: The passage explicitly describes it as hiding death, not harmlessness.

options.text: Her guests become wealthy and secure.
options.note: The passage's outcome is death, not wealth or security.

options.text: Her house offers temporary pleasure with no lasting effect either way.
options.note: The passage insists the effect is lasting and fatal, not neutral or temporary.

quiz.q: How does Wisdom's feast in this chapter anticipate Christ?

options.text: Christ calls Himself the bread of life and offers a table prepared at the cost of His own body and blood.
options.note: John 6:35 and the Last Supper directly echo this chapter's image of a costly, life giving feast freely offered.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament at all.
options.note: The invitation and bread and wine imagery are picked up directly in the Gospels.

options.text: It shows that Christ's invitation is only for the already wise.
options.note: Both Wisdom's invitation and Christ's own ministry specifically target the simple, the lost, and those lacking, not only the wise.

options.text: It refers only to a literal historical banquet with no further significance.
options.note: This underplays the deliberate, developed connection Scripture draws between this feast and the gospel's invitation to Christ's table.

questions: Wisdom's invitation and Folly's invitation use almost identical words. What temptations in your life look, on the surface, just as appealing as something genuinely good?
Wisdom spares no expense to prepare her feast and call in the simple. Where do you see God's generosity toward you, even before you had anything to offer in return?
Verse 10 restates the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom, exactly as in chapter 1. Has this truth become more or less central to how you actually make decisions since you first learned it?
Folly's guests do not realize the dead are in her house until it is too late. What warning signs are you tempted to ignore because the immediate pleasure feels sweet, like stolen water, verse 17?

Christ invites the simple and those lacking judgment to His own table, prepared at His own cost. What would it look like to come to Him honestly today, without pretending to already be wise or capable on your own?

translationNotes.note: Some ancient versions, the Septuagint, Syriac, and Aramaic Targum, read 'set up' rather than 'built,' a minor variation that does not change the overall picture of Wisdom's established house.
Some ancient versions read 'through Me' rather than 'through wisdom,' making Wisdom's own voice, rather than the abstract idea, the direct speaker of this promise.
